extracted.intended_audience: agency policymakers, regulatory scholars, and rulemaking practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the democratic role of public comments in administrative rulemaking and on how agencies should manage, evaluate, and respond to large volumes of comments (including bots, misinformed submissions, and mass campaigns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize democratic benefits of public comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comments evidence the public's hunger to participate in government and can importantly inform agency policy choices and make government more democratic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat high volumes of comment submissions merely as noise; appreciate that they can supply views and preferences relevant to value-laden policy decisions (e.g., dignity, quality of life, public resource uses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter false and bot comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must filter false comments and those submitted by bots from their dockets and act to deter them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filtering is a necessary management task because fraudulent or automated submissions can overwhelm dockets and distort the record; agencies should develop methods to detect and remove such submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not discourage genuine individual comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of 'mass' comments should not lead agencies to discourage even genuine individual comments or treat rulemaking as a plebiscite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid policies that blunt public participation; recognize legal protections and normative value of individual expressions of views even when many are similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider comments expressing views as relevant and legally protectable
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrative Procedure Act entitles 'interested persons' to submit 'written data, views, or arguments,' and agencies cannot legally refuse to consider comments expressing views rather than technical data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separateability of 'views' vs 'data' is unlikely and irrelevant to the obligation to consider submissions; do not create policies that exclude viewpoint-only comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value disclosed commenter identity for context
rubrics_metrics.description: A commenter's disclosed identity can provide important context to the decision-making agency (e.g., someone with a prosthetic leg commenting on ADA rules, or a resident of a polluted neighborhood commenting on air quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where identity is disclosed, agencies should account for the lived experience or stake that informs the comment; identity can affect the comment's probative value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and answer comments, even briefly
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should acknowledge and respond to comments on the record, even with brief answers, to convey that individuals have been heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Department of Defense response on sexual assault prevention and FCC responses in net neutrality rulemakings; brief replies that explain why views were accepted or not improve legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate openly about which comments are most relevant/helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must communicate to the public which kinds of comments will be most useful in a rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear guidance about relevance helps focus submissions and reduces wasted effort; publish instructions or examples of helpful comment content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comments to enhance democratic responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comments support agency democratic responsiveness by supplying issue-specific views that elected officials and oversight processes may miss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat comment input as a complementary channel to elections and oversight for conveying public preferences on specific rule proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment process can increase inclusiveness and representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenting offers individuals—especially those underrepresented by race, ethnicity, gender identity, resources, or other reasons—a chance to participate and can counterbalance dominance by regulated entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design processes and outreach to lower barriers to participation so that the docket better represents affected communities; view comment processes as civic education opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that large volumes can reveal overlooked perspectives or widespread misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: A large volume of individual comments may signal unnoticed or under-communicated perspectives or reveal public misunderstanding and misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When many comments raise the same points or misconceptions, agencies might pause to investigate, engage in outreach, or address misinformation rather than simply discarding the pattern as irrelevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to misinformed comments with public education and targeted outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may address widespread misunderstandings through outreach, focus groups, or public information campaigns rather than altering regulatory decisions based on misinformed pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: DOT convened focus groups and ran an information campaign about airbags instead of permitting widespread deactivation; use education to improve understanding and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance public views with statutory factors and technical expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking is not a plebiscite; agencies must weigh public views alongside statutory mandates, technical evidence, and other legal factors, and sometimes public preferences must yield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document how views were considered and why ultimately accepted or not, tying decisions to statute, evidence, and agency expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure comment integrity and invest in management systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should focus on the management challenges of ensuring comment integrity and on systems to handle large volumes of submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in infrastructure, triage processes, and procedures to sort, verify, and surface substantive comments while removing spam and abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dismiss comments solely because language matches group templates
rubrics_metrics.description: A comment's use of language suggested by advocacy groups should not automatically invalidate it; well-funded organizations often professionally draft comments that still express genuine individual views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess content and context rather than authorship patterns alone; look for indications that the submission communicates an individual's perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage comments to inform elected officials and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments in agency proceedings can inform elected officials who may not otherwise have systematic access to public views about a particular issue, aiding congressional and executive decision-making and oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve and summarize public input in ways accessible to oversight bodies to improve broader governmental responsiveness.
